## Definition

Backpressure is the mechanism by which a slow downstream consumer signals an upstream producer to reduce its emission rate, rather than letting an unbounded buffer grow until the process runs out of memory. It is a critical flow control mechanism in streaming pipelines and distributed systems where data flows asynchronously between components.

## Implementation Strategies

### Bounded Queues
The producer pushes items into a queue with a fixed maximum size. Once the queue is full, the producer blocks (or waits) until the consumer drains sufficient items, freeing space in the queue. This approach is simple and prevents unbounded memory growth.

### Credit-Based Flow Control
The consumer explicitly grants the producer permission to send N more items (a "credit" or "allowance"). As the consumer processes items, it sends feedback to the producer increasing its credit. The producer may only send when it has remaining credits. This is common in protocols like gRPC and Akka Streams.

### Reactive-Pull Models
Instead of the producer pushing data to the consumer, the consumer actively requests items on its own schedule. This inverts the control flow—the consumer "pulls" data rather than the producer "pushing" it. The producer never sends unsolicited data and thus cannot overwhelm the consumer. This model is used in RxJava, Project Reactor, and other reactive streams implementations.

## Importance

Without backpressure, fast producers can fill system memory with buffered items faster than slow consumers can drain them, leading to out-of-memory errors and system failure. Backpressure ensures that data flow rates adapt naturally to the slowest component in the pipeline.

## Related Patterns

- [[reactive-streams]] — standard protocols for asynchronous stream processing with backpressure
- [[flow-control]] — broader category of mechanisms to manage data rates
